title: What Delta and Psi Were Standing In For
standfirst: László Mednyánszky wrote his private diaries in German and Hungarian, but in the Greek alphabet, so that two letters — one for sex, one for spirituality — could carry the twenty-five years he spent loving a soldier named Bálint Kurdi. This calm, blossoming Nagyőr canvas was painted almost exactly in the middle of that unrecorded relationship.

sections.heading: Two Letters Doing the Work of a Language He Didn't Trust
sections.body:
Mednyánszky filled thousands of diary pages in German and Hungarian, the two languages he actually spoke, but he wrote them in the Greek alphabet — not translated into Greek, just transliterated into Greek letters, a schoolroom trick turned into a lock. Two symbols recur often enough that later readers could work out what they stood for: Δ, delta, for sex or physical contact; Ψ, psi, for spirituality. The cipher wasn't decorative. Hungary criminalized homosexual acts throughout Mednyánszky's adult life, and a landowning baron with a public reputation as a war correspondent and society portraitist had more than most to lose from a diary anyone could read straight off the page.

He didn't spell out what the code was protecting until 1912, when he [copied into his journal](https://spectator.sme.sk/culture-and-lifestyle/c/a-gay-painter-lost-his-love-their-relationship-continued-in-diaries) a passage arguing that homosexuality, understood rightly, 'leads to awakening and freedom instead of suffering' rather than damnation — a line he seems to have read as permission, decades into living by exactly that logic in private.

sections.heading: A Soldier in a Vienna Barracks, 1881
sections.body: The relationship the cipher was built to protect started in Vienna in 1881, when Mednyánszky — then twenty-nine — met a twenty-one-year-old serving in the local barracks named Bálint Kurdi and asked him to pose. Other accounts describe Kurdi [later working the Danube](https://bitterwinter.org/laszlo-mednyanszky-art-theosophy-and-a-homoerotic-new-religion/) as a boatman, a detail the barracks story doesn't rule out so much as leave for a different chapter of the same life; nothing in what survives pins down exactly when one occupation gave way to the other. What is consistent across every account is the length of what followed: the two men's friendship ran twenty-five years, through Kurdi's own marriage to a woman, until his death in 1906. Mednyánszky's diaries name him 'Nyuli' — Hungarian for bunny — the whole way through.

sections.heading: A Grave Bought Beside His, Never Used
sections.body:
Kurdi died of pneumonia in 1906. Mednyánszky paid for his tombstone in the cemetery at Vác, north of Budapest, then bought the adjoining plot for himself and kept returning to visit it. A found object became scripture: in December 1907, close to a year after the death, he came across a matchbox printed with a rabbit and read it as a message from Kurdi. By 1908 he was writing lines like 'The old dog [the painter] belongs to Nyuli' and had resolved, despite recorded doubts about whether he deserved it, to be buried at Kurdi's side.

The art historian István Bardoly, who prepared the diaries for a [2019 Slovak National Gallery edition](https://spectator.sme.sk/culture-and-lifestyle/c/a-gay-painter-lost-his-love-their-relationship-continued-in-diaries) after the first published selection had quietly cut the prayers addressed to Kurdi, found that none of this was as secret locally as the cipher suggests Mednyánszky feared. Kurdi was already known in Vác as the black sheep of his family, Bardoly noted, and his relationship with the painter, like his own inclinations, had never really been hidden from the town. Mednyánszky died in Vienna in April 1919 and was buried in Budapest's Kerepesi Cemetery. The plot beside Kurdi went unused.

sections.heading: A Landscape From the Calm Middle of the Story
sections.body:
Nothing in the record ties this particular canvas to Kurdi — no diary entry names it, no letter mentions painting it, and the honest thing to do with that silence is leave it alone rather than invent a connection the sources don't support. What can be said is the date. Blossoming Trees was painted around 1900, at Nagyőr, the family estate Mednyánszky kept returning to until that same year — which puts it almost exactly at the midpoint of the twenty-five years he spent with Kurdi, six years before the death that turned the relationship into a diary kept for a dead man.

It also sits at an awkward point stylistically for a piece filed simply under Impressionism. Mednyánszky's early landscapes were grey and melancholic, [shaped by Corot and the Barbizon painters](https://www.wga.hu/bio_m/m/mednyans/biograph.html); a visit to the Szolnok artists' colony in 1877 brought him into contact with August von Pettenkofen and lightened his palette, and three further years in France from 1889 pushed it toward the airy, broken brushwork the label implies. But from around 1895, back at Nagyőr, symbolist and mystical elements had already begun to dominate his work — the same environment, by more than one account, that fed his interest in Theosophy and the spiritual meanings it assigned to colour. A blossoming orchard painted in 1900 catches the bright manner on its way toward the darker, stranger work that would follow. 'Impressionism' describes the brushwork; it undersells the moment.

sections.heading: The Diary That Explained the Seclusion
sections.body:
For decades after Mednyánszky's death, biographers had an easy word for the long stretches he spent at Nagyőr, and later at the front as a war correspondent in Galicia, Serbia and the South Tyrol from 1914: temperament. He was the eccentric baron who preferred tramps and soldiers to salons, and who painted the destitute with more sympathy than he seems to have shown his own class. Bardoly's 2019 edition, restoring what the first published selection had cut, reframed that eccentricity as something more specific — a man who had built an entire private register of prayer and mourning around one dead boatman-soldier, in an alphabet chosen so that nobody else could read it.

The reframing doesn't touch the paintings themselves; Blossoming Trees looks exactly as it did before anyone published the diaries. It changes what the seclusion behind it was actually for.
